steps.name: 1️⃣ MICRO-CLUMPS — 2–5 KNOWN THINGS
steps.goal: Java learns that one completed behavior does not always produce immediate reinforcement; sometimes another known behavior follows first.
steps.actions:
Build tiny combinations from already-fluent pieces.

Examples:

Check in → short heel → reward

Short heel → halt → heel → reward

Group entry → one little loop → heel out → reward

Short heel → Sit in Motion with abbreviated walk-away → return → reward

Recall → Front → Finish → reward

Keep the behaviors shorter/easier than their maximum trained versions.

Canemo specifically says behaviors inside early clumps should be shortened to reduce mistakes. Canemo - Trained To Trial.pdf

Start from different points in the BH rather than always beginning at Check In.

No corrections inside the clump. Corrections change the picture you’re trying to show Java. Canemo - Trained To Trial.pdf

🎁 Reinforcer

Toy, with strategic food reinforcement available when you want to reinforce inside a longer sequence without completely breaking the trial-like flow. Canemo specifically describes intermittent food inside clumps for this purpose.
steps.description:
This is the first actual change in the reinforcement picture.

Canemo’s beginner clump is 2–5 things before reward, with their example:

heel onto field → check in → heel away 5 steps → reward. Canemo - Trained To Trial.pdf

The important question isn’t duration yet.

It’s:

Can Java finish one known thing and immediately remain available for the next known thing?
steps.todayJob: Two to five known things. Then party.
steps.criterion:
Java can perform small combinations of established behaviors without her engagement, understanding, or technical picture falling apart simply because reinforcement didn’t occur after the first behavior.

Transitions between those behaviors remain understandable and functional.
steps.rule:
➡️ Advance When

The question is no longer “Can Java do two or three things before reinforcement?”

She clearly can.

Now increase the amount of connected work—but do not permanently leave micro-clumps behind.

steps.name: 2️⃣ SMALL CLUMPS — CONNECT TRANSITIONS
steps.goal: Java learns the transitions between the major BH behaviors.
steps.actions:
Build short sequences specifically around transitions.

Examples:

Group → heel out → halt → heel

Heel → halt → Sit in Motion

Sit pickup/basic → heel

Heel → Down in Motion → recall

Recall → Front → Finish → basic

Long Down pickup → heel away → wait at starting point

Start from different locations on the BH road.

Canemo explicitly says not to always start at the beginning because otherwise the only way to reach later transitions is to continually perform everything preceding them. Canemo - Trained To Trial.pdf

Shorten heeling and walk-away distances during most clumps.

You are training connection, not proving maximum duration every repetition.

🎁 Reinforcer

Toy or strategically placed food.
steps.description:
Canemo makes an important point here:

Every transition from one behavior to the next should eventually have been shown to the dog.

This is where we deliberately make sure there aren’t weird black holes between individually trained exercises.
steps.todayJob: Find the seams between exercises and teach Java that the seams are part of the routine too.
steps.criterion: Java can move cleanly between the major established BH behaviors without confusion, disengagement, anticipation, or requiring extra handler help at the transitions.
steps.rule:
➡️ Advance When

The important transitions have been deliberately shown and Java remains available for the next behavior rather than mentally checking out after completing the previous one.

steps.name: 3️⃣ INTERMEDIATE CLUMPS — 5–10 THINGS
steps.goal: Java maintains the established training picture through a meaningful portion of the BH before reinforcement.
steps.actions:
Build larger combinations from fluent material.

Keep maximum-duration pieces abbreviated.

For example:

Group → heel out → halt → leash off → heel toward starting point → reward

or

Short off-leash heel → halt → Sit in Motion with shorter walk-away → return → basic → heel → reward

or

Down in Motion → abbreviated walk-away → recall → Front → Finish → heel → reward.

Vary where the clump begins and ends.

Sometimes pay earlier.

Sometimes later.

Don’t let Java know:

“Once we’ve done X, the toy always appears.”

🎁 Reinforcer

Toy, plus strategically placed food where useful.

Canemo recommends keeping reward placement variable and specifically preserving high reward expectation around areas such as about turns, slow heeling, group entry, check-in, and distractions.
steps.description:
Canemo’s intermediate guideline is approximately 5–10 things before reward. Their example includes:

group loop → halt/leash off → heel to start → heel forward → halt/leave in sit → return to basic → heel forward → reward. Canemo - Trained To Trial.pdf

We’re now asking Java for genuine trial-like continuity—but still not the whole routine.
steps.todayJob: Ask for a real chunk of work—not the whole fucking BH.
steps.criterion: Java can perform approximately 5–10 connected, already-known elements while maintaining useful engagement, technical quality, responsiveness, and expectation of future reinforcement.
steps.rule:
➡️ Advance When

Intermediate clumps are exposing only small wobbles, rather than revealing that Java doesn’t actually understand one of the component behaviors or transitions.

steps.name: VARIABLE CLUMP SIZE — PUSH, THEN COME BACK DOWN
steps.goal: Java learns that workload is unpredictable and reinforcement remains possible throughout the routine.
steps.actions:
Deliberately vary workload.

One repetition might be:

heel → halt → reward.

Next:

group → halt → heel → Sit in Motion → return → heel → reward.

Next:

check in → five steps → reward.

Next session you might ask for a substantially larger chunk.

Then immediately return to tiny, highly reinforced work.

Do the same with heeling duration.

Canemo’s notes explicitly use this up/down approach when building toward full BH heeling rather than making every surrounding repetition long. Canemo - Trained To Trial.pdf

🎁 Reinforcer

Toy / food strategically and unpredictably placed.
steps.description:
This is probably the most important Canemo clumping principle:

Do not progress linearly.

Canemo repeatedly says to increase, then come back down. Bigger clumps do not replace smaller clumps.

So this is NOT:

3 things → 5 → 7 → 10 → 15 → whole BH forever.

It’s:

small → medium → tiny → larger → small → medium → tiny.
steps.todayJob: Push up. Come back down. Keep hope fucking alive.
steps.criterion:
A larger clump does not cause Java to assume that future repetitions will also be long, and smaller clumps continue producing strong expectation and expression.

Java remains willing to work because reinforcement is still genuinely unpredictable.
steps.rule:
➡️ Advance When

Java comfortably handles variable clump sizes and increasing workload without the emotional or technical picture progressively eroding.

steps.name: 5️⃣ USE CLUMPING AS A DIAGNOSTIC
steps.goal: Larger connected pictures reveal weaknesses without Kerrie trying to repair those weaknesses inside the clump.
steps.actions:
Run an appropriate clump.

Don’t nag Java through it.

If something small gets imperfect—slightly crooked, slightly less precise—note it and keep going when appropriate.

If something major fails—wrong behavior, loss of understanding, serious emotional deterioration—end/modify the clumping question rather than drilling failure.

Afterward identify:

🐕 Dog issue?
🧠 Handler issue?
🧩 Component-training hole?
🔗 Transition problem?
⏱️ Duration problem?

Then train the weak piece separately.

Next time, put it back into an easier clump and see whether the repair survives.

🎁 Reinforcer

Normal strategic clumping reinforcement.
steps.description:
Canemo explicitly calls clumping a measurement.

When pieces are connected, you’ll often get a wobble. That’s useful information.

Their instruction is essentially:

notice it → write it down → repair it separately → put it back into a clump later. Canemo - Trained To Trial.pdf
steps.todayJob: Clump to find holes. Repair holes somewhere else.
steps.criterion:
Kerrie can use clumping to identify weaknesses without turning every clump into an impromptu correction/detail session.

Weaknesses improve when separately repaired and subsequently reintroduced.
steps.rule:
➡️ Advance When

The remaining wobbles are increasingly about routine duration/trial presentation, rather than missing component understanding.

steps.name: 6️⃣ LARGE / NEAR-TRIAL CLUMPS
steps.goal: Java can perform substantial portions of the BH in realistic trial presentation without continuous reinforcement or handler assistance.
steps.actions:
Connect substantial sections of the BH.

Examples:

Check in → waiting → on-leash heel section → group → transition/leash removal → off-leash heel → reward.

Or start later:

Sit in Motion → pickup → heel → Down with Recall → Front → Finish → reward.

Or:

Long Down pickup → heel to starting position → wait → begin work → reward.

Use normal trial handling.

Don’t carry training aids into the clump that won’t exist in trial.

Canemo specifically warns against constantly nagging with the leash because you won’t have that option in the trial picture. Canemo - Trained To Trial.pdf

🎁 Reinforcer

Toy, strategically located after the chosen clump.
steps.description:
Now the pieces can become genuinely large.

But Canemo still recommends abbreviating the biggest duration sinks during many clumps—particularly long heeling and walking away from the dog—because longer duration creates more opportunities for errors.
steps.todayJob: Show Java a big piece of trial without showing her the whole damn movie every time.
steps.criterion: Java can perform substantial BH sections with normal trial handling while preserving functional technical quality, engagement, and emotional resilience through the connected work.
steps.rule:
➡️ Advance When

The full routine is now an appropriate occasional proof of the assembled behavior, rather than an attempt to discover whether the behaviors exist.

steps.name: 7️⃣ OCCASIONAL FULL BH PICTURE
steps.goal: Java has experienced the complete BH obedience routine before trial without learning that full unrewarded routines are normal training.
steps.actions:
Occasionally run the complete obedience picture with:

* trial entry/check-in,
* trial handling,
* actual transitions,
* realistic reinforcement absence,
* no corrections,
* no unnecessary help.

Observe.

Record the holes.

Then go back to training.

After a full-routine exposure, return to:
tiny clumps, high-value detail work, strategic reinforcement, and shorter duration.

Do not respond to successful full BH by running another fucking full BH tomorrow.

🎁 Reinforcer

Major reward after completion, followed in subsequent sessions by a return to much higher reinforcement density.
steps.description:
Canemo allows for showing the complete BH because it is a relatively small routine—but specifically warns not to do it frequently or immediately before the trial.

Their notes recommend showing the complete routine roughly 2–3 weeks before trial, then dropping workload again so the dog approaches trial with a high expectation of reinforcement. Canemo - Trained To Trial.pdf

This is proofing, not your new training format.
steps.todayJob: Show the whole picture once. Learn from it. Then get the hell back out of it.
steps.criterion: Java can perform the complete assembled BH obedience routine with normal trial handling and without needing reinforcement/correction within every individual exercise, while retaining a recognizable version of the emotional and technical picture built in training.
steps.rule:
➡️ Advance When

There isn’t another Clumping rung.

From here, use variable clump sizes + detail work + occasional trial-picture exposure according to what Java’s performance tells you.

components.name: TRIAL ASSEMBLY
components.finishedPicture:
Basic requirements for the dog’s behavior / performance in all levels of the trial. Expressive behavior/self-confidence. Particular attention is to be paid to expressive behavior by the dog during the judging and by awarding the respective score. The dogs must show that they want to do the required exercise for the handler and not show that they are being pressured to do it. Close observation of the entire dog such as facial expression, ear and tail position, tense muscles, unnatural movement, excessive breathing rate, excessive salivation, or hectic behavior, etc., contribute to the evaluation. Negative
reactions after the delivery of verbal commands leads to deductions.
Free, happy, motivated work The dog should show motivated work. A strong willingness to work and to show a performance / execution of the work is top priority.
Concentration/attention
The dog must be concentrated / attentive to the handler during the entire routine without showing an extremely abnormal body or head posture (unnatural or robotic movement).
Harmony of the team
The presentation should show strong harmony in its work between the dog and handler. The dog
must be able to follow the handler in a normal manner.
Technical correctness/position
In addition to natural expressive behavior and a harmonious performance, attention must be paid to the technically correct execution of the exercise. The exercises should be performed clearly and according to their description.
Acceptance of commands and execution of an exercise The dog should always accept the commands immediately and perform the exercises without stress or delay.
Basic assessment in the execution of trial exercises
When assessing an exercise, a distinction must be made between the primary and the secondary
components. The primary part of an exercise is determined in all phases by the name of the
respective exercise. This is to ensure that the primary part of an exercise is reflected stronger in the assessment than mistakes in the secondary parts of an exercise.
The dog's response to the verbal command
The dog should perform the exercise freely, open behavior at the handler's verbal command. Any
behaviors showing stress or fear is faulty and will devalue the exercise.
Additional verbal commands
1st additional command (2nd command total) = 1.5 pt deduction, 2nd additional command (3rd total command) = 2.5 pt deduction. If a dog does not perform an exercise after the 2nd additional verbal command (3rd total), the exercise is to be awarded 0 points, “M”. If the dog performs the exercise incorrectly (e.g. standing/lying in the sitting exercise, sitting/standing in the down exercise, etc.), the exercise will be devalued at 50%.
If a dog performs the exercise before the verbal command, the exercise is to be evaluated with minus 2 points.
Execution of the basic position
The basic position is the sitting position of the dog on the left side of the handler. Each exercise
begins and ends with a basic position. The basic position may only be assumed once before each
exercise from the forward movement. In the basic position the dog must sit straight, attentive to the
handler, with its shoulder blade at knee height to the left of the handler. In the basic position, the
handler is not allowed to stand with his legs spread and both arms must be relaxed against the body.
Development /Build-up of an exercise
From the basic position the development is carried out in the exercises "Sit in motion", "Down with recall", "Stand exercise" and "Send out with down". It must be at least 10, but no more than 15 steps before the verbal command is given to perform the exercise.
Picking up / calling the dog
In all the exercises where the dog is picked up, the handler can approach the dog from the front or by
going around the dog from behind. When calling the dog, the dog's name may be used instead of the verbal command for approach. The dog's name in conjunction with the verbal command for
approach is considered a double command. The dog must approach happy, free, with purpose, fast and directly, it must and sit close and straight in front of the handler. At the verbal command for the basic position the dog must move directly to the end basic position. This can be done by the dog walking around the handler at the rear or with a “flip finish “moving to the basic position. If the
handler needs an additional verbal command for the dog to go into the final basic position, the
exercise is 1.5 points. if two additional verbal commands are required for this, a deduction of 2.5 points. If, after the second additional verbal command, the dog does not take the basic position, the entire exercise is to be rated as "Insufficient".
Praise
The dog may briefly be freed up and praised after each exercise. During the short praise and freeing
up (maximum of about 5 seconds), the dog may leave the basic position. After this praise/freeing
up, the dog must be back into the basic position and after showing at least about 3 seconds, the next exercise may start.
Report in for Obedience
At the beginning of the obedience exercise, both handlers and their dogs must present themselves to the judge. This is done with the dog on leash for the BH and IGP/USP 1, off leash for all other levels.
The handlers will report to the judge their name, the name of the dog and the title they are reporting in for.
Start and ending of an exercise
The judge gives the instruction for the start of an exercise. Failure of the handler to wait for the
judge’s signal to start an exercise is faulty and will incur a deduction. Handlers that intentionally start
/ execute exercises without the judge’s signal to start will be faulted more severely with a deduction (loss) of up to all points for the exercise (0 pts “M”). All other portions of the exercise like turns, stops changes in tempo etc. are performed without instructions of the judge. If the handler forgets an exercise, the judge will ask the handler to perform the forgotten exercise. There is no point devaluation for this. Forgotten partial exercises will devaluate the exercise.
🔥 The Canemo rule I would put in the component notes

CLUMPING IS NOT A LINEAR LADDER.

Even though FIELDWORK needs progression steps to organize development, once Java reaches the later stages you continue using the earlier steps.

Canemo’s actual philosophy is:

Detail → clump → detail → smaller clump → bigger clump → repair → tiny clump → big clump.

And I think that’s particularly important with Java because we are not sacrificing the emotional picture just to prove she can survive more minutes without a toy.

If a bigger clump starts eating the dog you actually want to walk onto the trial field with, the answer isn’t “she needs more fucking clumping.” The clump just gave you data.

exercises.name: TRIAL ASSEMBLY
exercises.criteria:
Java can move through the complete BH obedience routine as one connected trial picture, performing already-trained behaviors and their transitions without needing reinforcement or correction after every individual behavior.

She remains engaged, expressive, technically functional, and connected to Kerrie as reinforcement becomes less frequent and larger portions of the routine are connected.

Kerrie can present the routine in trial handling—without constantly helping, correcting, prompting, or changing her body before rewards.

Java does not merely memorize one giant predictable chain. Individual clumps can begin at different places, vary in length, and connect different portions of the routine while preserving the established behaviors and transitions.
exercises.notes:
📝 Prerequisite Notes

Clumping does not teach the component behaviors.

Before a behavior enters a clump, Kerrie should be satisfied that Java understands that behavior independently. Canemo specifically describes clumping as being ready to “abandon the details” temporarily and ask for multiple known behaviors without the normal reward/correction structure. Canemo - Trained To Trial.pdf

That means:

Heeling owns heeling.
Turns owns turns.
Group owns group.
Automatic Halt owns halt.
Sit in Motion owns sit.
Down with Recall owns down/recall.
Front owns front.
Finish owns finish.
Long Down owns long down.

Clumping owns connecting them.

If a component has a significant hole, repair it in its owning component before expecting it to survive a larger clump. Canemo specifically recommends skipping a weak piece, training it separately in detail, and then reincorporating it. Canemo - Trained To Trial.pdf

steps.name: 1️⃣ BUILD THE BUCKET DESTINATION
steps.goal: Java develops a powerful expectation of driving straight to the bucket to obtain the ball.
steps.actions:
Place the bucket straight downfield with the ball inside it.

Initially let Java understand that the bucket contains the ball.

Send her.

Build distance progressively while preserving:

straightness → speed → commitment → confidence.

Don’t introduce the Down question yet just because it’s part of the finished exercise.

Dave’s useful contribution here is to avoid accidentally building dependence on watching Kerrie place the reward. Once Java understands the destination, begin creating blind setups where the ball was already placed.

🎁 Reinforcer

Ball inside bucket.
steps.description:
This is Mario’s preferred foundation.

Ball goes INSIDE the bucket.

Dave’s primary-reward principle supports the same developmental question: first create a dog that fucking GOES. We’re using Mario’s bucket rather than Dave’s hanging-ball pole.
steps.todayJob: See destination → fucking GO.
steps.criterion: Java drives directly and enthusiastically to the bucket with no uncertainty about the job.
steps.rule:
➡️ Advance When

The bucket has become a strong destination and Java no longer needs to watch Kerrie place the ball to understand where she’s going.

steps.name: 2️⃣ BLIND SENDS — TRUST THE BUCKET
steps.goal: Java believes the ball can exist in the bucket without seeing it placed.
steps.actions:
Set the ball in the bucket before Java sees the setup.

Bring Java onto the field.

Send.

Ball is there.

Repeat enough to create genuine destination belief.

A helper can secretly reload the bucket while Java is returning/occupied if useful—the functional equivalent of Dave’s Magic Ball setup.

Vary repetition count rather than teaching one Send Out = session finished.

🎁 Reinforcer

Ball inside bucket.
steps.description:
This is where Dave’s blind send / magic-ball principle fits beautifully into Mario’s bucket system.

Java stops thinking:

“I watched Kerrie put a ball there.”

and starts thinking:

“That fucking bucket pays.”
steps.todayJob: Trust what you can’t see.
steps.criterion: Blind placement produces essentially the same committed Send Out as marked placement.
steps.rule:
➡️ Advance When

Java no longer needs visual confirmation that Kerrie placed the ball before she will commit fully to the bucket.

steps.name: 3️⃣ GENERALIZE THE BUCKET DESTINATION
steps.goal: Java understands the Send Out picture across fields rather than only on her familiar training field.
steps.actions:
New field:

Bucket + ball.

Let Java acquire the new destination picture and build successful sends.

Don’t use a novel field as the moment to prove that she understands an empty bucket.

Across training, vary:

* field,
* approach,
* background picture,
* distance,
* environmental landmarks.

But on new-field introduction, Mario’s rule wins:

ball in bucket.

🎁 Reinforcer

Ball inside bucket.
steps.description:
This comes directly from Mario:

Every time you go to a new field, put the ball in the bucket.

Dave independently emphasizes that a dog who understands the home field doesn’t automatically understand an arbitrary new field.

So we don’t test Java’s faith on first exposure to a new field. We pay the destination.
steps.todayJob: New field = make the destination fucking obvious and valuable.
steps.criterion: Java rapidly establishes the same straight, committed Send Out on different fields.
steps.rule:
➡️ Advance When

The Send Out concept is clearly portable and established fields are ready for the first empty-bucket question.

steps.name: 4️⃣ INTRODUCE THE EMPTY BUCKET → PLATZ
steps.goal: Java learns that sometimes the bucket is empty, and the absence of the ball predicts the Platz/reward-from-handler picture.
steps.actions:
Mix:

Ball in bucket → Send → Java gets ball.

and

Empty bucket → Send → Platz at destination → ball from Kerrie.

Do not make empty bucket the new permanent setup.

Do not always finish the session with the ball in the bucket either.

Mix the pictures so Java cannot solve the exercise by learning a rigid session pattern.

If the empty-bucket picture causes deterioration in the Send, increase paid-bucket history again rather than trying to correct more Send Out into her.

🎁 Reinforcer

Two possibilities:

Ball in bucket, or ball from Kerrie following Platz.
steps.description:
This is the critical Mario transition.

Sometimes there is no ball in the bucket.

Java still sends all the way there.

When the ball isn’t there, she Platzes.

Reinforcement now comes from Kerrie.

This starts creating the belief:

Ball present → get ball.

Ball absent → Platz → Kerrie produces ball.

And importantly, Mario says don’t correct during this process, specifically so we don’t introduce conflict into going.
steps.todayJob: Empty doesn’t mean you were wrong to go.
steps.criterion: Java reaches the empty bucket with the same commitment she shows when the ball is present and can Platz there without the absence of the ball creating conflict or disappointment that damages subsequent sends.
steps.rule:
➡️ Advance When

The empty-bucket → Platz → handler reward picture is understood and mixing it with ball-in-bucket reps does not materially weaken the Send.

steps.name: 5️⃣ AUTO-PLATZ AT THE EMPTY BUCKET
steps.goal: The empty bucket itself begins producing the Platz response.
steps.actions:
Continue mixing:

paid bucket

and

empty bucket.

Watch what Java does when she arrives and finds no ball.

Give her room to solve the known picture rather than racing in with unnecessary help.

When she produces the expected Platz, reinforcement comes from Kerrie.

Continue paying plenty of actual bucket sends.

Do not turn auto-Platz into a reason to stop paying the bucket.

🎁 Reinforcer

Ball from Kerrie following the empty-bucket Platz; ball in bucket on paid reps.
steps.description:
Mario’s progression is that with enough alternating experience, Java should begin to auto-Platz when she discovers that the bucket is empty.

That’s useful because it tells us the two reward contingencies have become clear to her.
steps.todayJob: No ball? I know the other answer.
steps.criterion: On empty-bucket repetitions, Java independently begins offering the Platz while maintaining the same drive toward the destination.
steps.rule:
➡️ Advance When

Auto-Platz at the empty bucket is clearly understood and, critically, Java is still driving hard enough that introducing an earlier Platz is unlikely to poison the Send.

steps.name: 6️⃣ INTRODUCE THE MID-FIELD PLATZ — RARELY
steps.goal: 6️⃣ INTRODUCE THE MID-FIELD PLATZ — RARELY
steps.actions:
Continue normal bucket sends.

Then occasionally:

Send → Java commits downfield → Platz ¼–½ downfield → reward from Kerrie.

Mario’s approximate ratio from your notes is:

about one partial/mid-field Platz for every three sends.

Treat that as his training guideline, not a mathematical law you must obey forever.

The surrounding repetitions continue protecting the destination drive.

🎁 Reinforcer

Ball from Kerrie after the mid-field Platz; bucket ball continues on the destination reps.
steps.description:
Now Mario moves the Down forward.

Send Java toward the bucket and occasionally cue Platz approximately ¼–½ of the way downfield.

This is not something we start hammering.

Mario specifically says this trial-type picture should be done rarely.
steps.todayJob: Run like you’re going all the fucking way—and listen if Kerrie says otherwise.
steps.criterion:
Java can be interrupted mid-send with Platz without beginning to anticipate it on subsequent sends.

Her next full Send Out remains fast, straight and committed.
steps.rule:
➡️ Advance When

Mid-field Platz is responsive while the full-distance Send Out remains emotionally unchanged.

steps.name: 7️⃣ BALANCE THE TWO EXPECTATIONS
steps.goal: Java genuinely does not know whether this repetition ends with the bucket reward or a Platz/reward from Kerrie—and therefore remains committed to both going and listening.
steps.actions:
Mix intelligently:

Send → ball in bucket.

Send → empty bucket → Platz → handler reward.

Occasional Send → mid-field Platz → handler reward.

Don’t establish a predictable alternation.

Don’t always end with the ball in the bucket.

Don’t always end with a Platz.

Ball either at destination or from Kerrie, according to that repetition’s question.
steps.description:
This is where Mario’s system accomplishes the useful part of Dave’s pendulum without adopting Dave’s correction approach.

We need:

🔥 GO

without losing

“Maybe I shouldn’t really go because she’s about to stop me.”

sometimes destination ball,

On a new field, go back to Mario’s rule:

ball in the bucket.

Don’t use trial assembly as an excuse to stop maintaining destination reward history.

🎁 Reinforcer

Ball at bucket and ball from Kerrie according to the training question.
steps.description:
Only now do we care about assembling the surrounding exercise picture.

This is where Dave’s sequencing material becomes useful again: don’t prematurely make heeling part of Send Out development.

The Send Out and Down exist first.

Then the trial setup consumes them.

components.name: Send out with down
components.finishedPicture:
From the required exercise setup, Java drives fast, straight, committed and confidently downfield on the Send Out cue, trusting the destination even though she does not know whether the ball is waiting there.

On the Down cue, Java immediately and confidently Platz, including when cued approximately ¼–½ of the way downfield for the trial picture.

The Down does not create hesitation in the Send Out. Java does not leave Kerrie wondering whether she should run or anticipate the Platz. She drives because the Send Out itself has enormous reward history and she trusts that reinforcement can exist either at the destination or from Kerrie after the Platz.

No correction conflict attached to going.
🔥 Key distinction for FIELDWORK

I would put this in the global notes because it prevents you from accidentally fucking this up six months from now:

Mario owns the reinforcement architecture. Dave supplements the mechanics.

The bucket is the destination. New fields get a ball in the bucket. Empty bucket develops trust in handler-delivered reinforcement and the Platz. Mid-field Platz is introduced only after the empty-bucket picture is understood and is trained rarely. No corrections are attached to the Send Out because we do not create conflict with going.

Dave’s useful additions are marked → blind development, destination belief, high reward history, multiple sends, field generalization, delaying heeling/assembly, and the conceptual need to balance GO with DOWN.

exercises.name: SEND OUT WITH DOWN
exercises.criteria:
Send out with down
1st part: Basic position, build-up, execution of the send out portion, 50% of the points.
2nd part: After instruction from the judge, downing, final basic position, 50% of the points.
From a basic position and on the instruction of the judge, the handler starts the exercise. After a verbal command for heeling, the team starts in a normal gait and in a straight line for about 10 -15
paces. After this 10 – 15 paces the handler gives a verbal command for going out. On the single command for going out while raising the arm, the handler stands still and sends his/her dog out. Then the dog must take a run in a straight path in the shown direction for a minimum of 20 meters. At the instruction of the judge, the handler gives the command for the dog to down, which must be executed
immediately. The handler is allowed to hold the arm up in the direction of the exercise until the dog has downed.
If the dog does not go down on the first command, the handler must independently give a second command within three seconds, this is the same for the third command.
At the direction of the judge, the handler goes to his dog and stands right next to him. At the
instruction of the judge, the handler gives the command for the dog to sit. The dog must sit quickly, straight and clam in the basic position.
exercises.notes:
Evaluation criteria
Primary evaluation:
The way out (direct, straight, and fast running ahead) and the direct reaction and execution of the verbal command to go down.
Secondary evaluation:
mistakes in the build-up, restless while down and mistakes in the pickup and final basic position.
Faults
Handler help leads to further deductions.
If the dog does not go the minimum distance or cannot be stopped with 3 commands, the exercise receives 0 points
Dog stops on first command but does not down, downs immediately on second command -1.5 points.
Dog stops on first command but does not down, downs immediately on third command -2.5 points.
Dog stops on first command but does not down on third command. -3.5 points.
Dog does not stop on first command, stops and downs immediately on second command -2.5 points.
Dog doesn’t stop on 1st or 2nd command, stops and down immediately on 3rd command -3.5 points.
Dog cannot be stopped with 3 commands. 0 point.
Dog downs directly on the first command, but after the judge's instructions to go pick- up the dog,
the dog breaks, if the dog can be stopped by a maximum of 50% of the distance to the dog handler. up to -5 points.
Additional mistakes are also deducted.
If the dog returns to the handler for more than 50% of the distance, the exercise is valuated with 0 points. Faults in the build-up, slow or unsure going forward, delayed stopping, slow down, restless down as well as mistakes in the pick-up, and basic position lead to additional deductions.

steps.name: 1️⃣ STEADY THROUGH THE THROW
steps.goal: Java remains independently in basic position while Kerrie throws.
steps.actions:
Java in basic.

Kerrie rehearses throwing motion while Java remains seated.

Then:

throw dumbbell → Java remains seated → release → retrieve/play.

Dave uses a tab initially so breaking cannot pay.

You can also use his variation:

throw → wait → step away → return → release.

That is particularly useful because we’re not merely teaching Java to wait for a predictable 2-second countdown. We’re teaching:

Nothing except the release means GO.

Dave personally asks for handler eye contact before release. That’s optional, not part of the FCI requirement. I wouldn’t make that a new requirement unless you actually want it.

🎁 Reinforcer

Release to ball/retrieve + play.
steps.description:
📝 Description

This is Dave’s capping work.

We’re isolating the thing that needs cleaning rather than contaminating Java’s existing dumbbell retrieve.
steps.todayJob: The throw is not the fucking cue.
steps.criterion: Kerrie can make a realistic throwing motion and throw while Java remains calmly and independently in basic position until released.

➡️ Advance When

steps.name: 2️⃣ TRANSFER STEADINESS TO THE DUMBBELL
steps.goal: Java gives the same capped response when the real dumbbell is thrown.
steps.actions:
Basic → throw dumbbell → wait → Retrieve cue.

Vary the delay before sending.

Occasionally throw and don’t immediately retrieve: pause, reset your own posture, then send.

Keep Kerrie’s throwing mechanics clean because current rules require the dumbbell to land within a 4 × 4 m square beginning 8 m from the basic position. If it lands outside, an assistant places it in the center before the Retrieve command can be given. The command can’t be given until the dumbbell has stopped moving—or, if repositioned, until the assistant is behind Kerrie’s position. 

🎁 Reinforcer

The retrieve itself + terminal toy/play as appropriate.
steps.description:
Now we put the dumbbell back in without changing the question.

We’re not retraining the retrieve.

We’re asking whether Java’s new throw-control survives the object that carries much more retrieve history.
steps.todayJob: Dumbbell flying through the air changes nothing until Kerrie says Retrieve.
steps.criterion: Java remains quiet and steady through realistic dumbbell throws, then leaves immediately on the actual Retrieve cue.
steps.rule:
➡️ Advance When

There is a clear distinction between:

throw = stay

and

Retrieve = explode.

steps.name: 3️⃣ FAST OUTBOUND + IMMEDIATE PICKUP
steps.goal: Clean up the front half of Java’s existing retrieve without changing her hold.
steps.actions:
Run isolated retrieves where the only question is:

release → fucking GO → direct line → immediate pickup.

Don’t bury a mediocre outbound underneath praise for a pretty Front.

Conversely, don’t start screwing around with Java’s known hold because you’re trying to improve speed.

If the outbound loses intensity, change reinforcement/play structure rather than turning the dumbbell into obedience drudgery.

🎁 Reinforcer

Toy/play, using Java’s existing retrieve reinforcement structure.
steps.description: Current FCI rules specifically want the dog to run directly to the dumbbell and pick it up immediately, with motivated, determined movement. Slow, unmotivated or indirect work and faulty pickup cost points.
steps.todayJob: Retrieve means ATTACK THE JOB.
steps.criterion: Immediate departure, fast purposeful direct line, immediate clean pickup.
steps.rule:
➡️ Advance When

The outbound and pickup are no longer the meaningful point loss.

steps.name: 4️⃣ TIGHT TURNAROUND
steps.goal: Java picks up and turns directly back toward Kerrie rather than looping around the dumbbell.
steps.actions:
Throw/place the dumbbell into a constrained area:

fence corner / wall configuration / puppy-box-type setup.

Java can reach the dumbbell normally but does not have enough room to make the big sweeping arc.

She:

arrives → grips → turns → comes the fuck back.

Build enough repetition that the movement pattern becomes habitual.

Then progressively remove the physical constraint.

Don’t make the environmental prop permanent.

🎁 Reinforcer

Strong reward back at Kerrie.
steps.description:
This is Dave’s fence/corner/puppy-box drill.

It directly supports the current rule picture: pickup immediately → turn directly → return directly.
steps.todayJob: Grab. Flip. Return.
steps.criterion: Java’s default after pickup is an immediate, efficient turn back toward Kerrie rather than an outward loop.
steps.rule:
➡️ Advance When

The tight turnaround survives removal of the environmental constraint.

steps.name: 5️⃣ RETURN SPEED → STRAIGHT FRONT
steps.goal: Java returns as powerfully as she went out without sacrificing the established Front.
steps.actions:
Retrieve → tight turn → accelerate home → established Front.

Use Dave’s idea of rewarding through/behind Kerrie selectively if you need more return commitment, because Java already understands that reward geography.

But don’t let that create:

“Blast through Kerrie instead of Front.”

Alternate appropriately between return-speed reinforcement and complete Front presentation.

If the Front gets crooked, repair Fronts.

If the return gets slow, repair Retrieve.

Don’t fucking solve one by ruining the other.

🎁 Reinforcer

Toy/play with strategic reward placement for return speed.
steps.description:
This matters under the current rules: FCI specifically wants motivated return speed comparable to the outbound, followed by a close Front/presentation. Bumping Kerrie is faulty. 

And this is why Dave cares about the turnaround—the pickup shouldn’t send Java onto a shitty return line that then makes the Front harder.

Your existing Front progression owns Front mechanics.

Retrieve simply consumes it.
steps.todayJob: Coming back matters just as much as going out.
steps.criterion: Java returns directly and with comparable motivation/speed to her outbound, then independently converts that speed into a close, straight Front without collision.
steps.rule:
➡️ Advance When

Fast return and accurate Front coexist rather than trading off.

steps.name: 6️⃣ PRESENTATION + OUT
steps.goal: Java’s already-trained hold survives the complete retrieve picture.
steps.actions:
Retrieve → Front → calm presentation ~3 sec → Out.

Vary training duration around the trial duration so Java doesn’t start anticipating Out from an internal stopwatch.

Kerrie takes the dumbbell cleanly.

Don’t repeatedly fiddle with it.

If Java’s known Hold deteriorates, go repair the Hold, then bring it back.

🎁 Reinforcer

Toy/play after clean presentation and release.
steps.description:
Again, we are not teaching Hold here.

We’re checking whether the known Hold remains clean after the excitement of a full retrieve.

Current FCI requires the dumbbell to be held firmly and calmly during retrieval and presentation until Kerrie commands release after approximately a 3-second pause. Java must allow Kerrie to take it promptly. Mouthing, playing, dropping, restless presentation and problems with the Out are faults.
steps.todayJob: Run like hell. Then shut the fuck up with your mouth. 😂
steps.criterion: Java arrives with energy but transitions into a firm, calm dumbbell presentation and releases immediately on the Out cue.
steps.rule:
➡️ Advance When

Retrieve arousal no longer materially affects grip quality or release.

steps.name: 7️⃣ COMPLETE FLAT RETRIEVE
steps.goal: All of Java’s established pieces survive as one scored exercise.
steps.actions:
Run:

Basic → throw → remain steady → dumbbell stops → Retrieve → fast/direct outbound → immediate pickup → tight/direct turn → fast/direct return → close straight Front → calm presentation ~3 sec → Out → pause ~3 sec → Finish/basic.

Kerrie then holds the dumbbell in the right hand, arm straight down, and ultimately returns it to the stand with Java heeling appropriately. 

Don’t respond to a mistake by repeatedly drilling the entire retrieve.

Identify the fucking leak:

breaking? → Steps 1–2
slow outbound/pickup? → 3
wide turn? → 4
slow/crooked return? → 5
hold/Out? → 6
Front? → Front progression
Finish? → Finish progression

Then repair that component.

🎁 Reinforcer

High-value toy/play after completion, with strategic reinforcement of individual pieces maintained outside full retrieves.

Now we assemble it.

steps.criterion: Java performs the entire flat retrieve with the current FCI priorities intact: steady start, immediate purposeful retrieve, direct pickup/turn, equally motivated return, clean close Front, firm calm presentation, willing Out and correct final basic position.

components.name: DUMBBELL RETRIEVE
components.finishedPicture:
From a straight, calm basic position, Kerrie throws the dumbbell into the required area while Java remains quietly and independently in basic position.

After the dumbbell has stopped moving and Kerrie gives the Retrieve command, Java leaves immediately, directly, fast and purposefully, picks the dumbbell up immediately, makes a direct tight turn, and returns to Kerrie with the same motivated, purposeful speed.

Java comes directly into a close, straight Front without bumping Kerrie and presents the dumbbell firmly and calmly. After approximately a 3-second presentation, she releases promptly on the Out command. After approximately another 3-second pause, she performs the Finish into correct final basic position.

No anticipation, breaking on the throw, wide turnaround, slow return, mouthing, playing, dropping, crooked Front, bumping, reluctant Out, restless presentation, or handler help.

Those are directly aligned with the current FCI judging priorities: the retrieve itself, motivated/direct outbound and return, pickup, close Front/presentation, calm firm hold, and clean Out are primary considerations; start/final basic positions are secondary.

exercises.name: Dumbbell Retrieve
exercises.criteria:
(IGP/USP 1 dumbbell weight 650 grams, IGP/USP 2 weight 1000 gm, IGP/USP 3 weight
A 4-meter by 4-meter square must be marked on the ground starting 8 meters from the basic position. With the dog sitting in a straight basic position the handler throws the dumbbell within this
square.
If the dumbbell lands outside the square, it is placed in the middle of the square by an assistant, who then moves behind the handler's position before the command to retrieve may be given.
If the handler’s foot moves while the handler throws the dumbbell no points are lost if it does not affect the dog. If the leg is moved during the throw, a 3 second pause must be shown after returning to basic position.
The verbal command “retrieve”/ “bring” may only be given when the dumbbell has stopped
moving or after the assistant is behind the handler.
On the verbal command for retrieving or bringing, the dog must run directly to the dumbbell, pick it up immediately, turn directly and return directly to the handler and present the dumbbell directly in the sit in front position. The aim is to show motivated and determined running towards the dumbbell and motivated returns. During the presentation of the dumbbell and also during the retrieving portion, the dumbbell must be held firmly and calmly until the handler commands the dog to release the dumbbell after about a 3 second pause in front. The dog needs to sit directly in front of the handler in a way the handler can easily take the dumbbell from the dog. Touching or
bumping the handler is faulty. The dog must present the dumbbell to the handler. After outing the dumbbell and an approx. 3 second pause, the dog is commanded into the final basic position. After outing the dumbbell, the dumbbell is held in the handler’s right hand with the arm straight down at handler’s side. After another 3 second pause, the handler gives the verbal command for the dog to
go into the final basic position. This may be accomplished by the dog either going around the handler or directly from the front to the left side of the handler into the basic position. The handler must then place the dumbbell back on the stand. During this part, the dog must heel with the handler
as described for “heeling.” For left-handed people, after permission from the judge to give the dog a “sit” command the handler may take one step to the right, throw the dumbbell, and then step back to
the dog to continue the exercise.
exercises.notes:
Primary evaluation:
in this exercise are: execution of the retrieve, motivated running to the dumbbell and then back to the dog handler with the same speed going out and returning, sitting close in front of the handler, and presenting the dumbbell, and the way the dog receives and responds to the out command.
Secondary evaluation:
are the executions of the start and final basic positions.
Faults
If the dog shows slow behavior, any form of stress, is unmotivated or not purposeful on the way out and/or return, has a faulty pick-up, drops the dumbbell, plays with or mouths the dumbbell, the handler has a splayed leg stance, there are mistakes in the presentation, errors in the sit in front
and/or in the basic positions (for example, restless behavior) as well as any dog handler help, there will be point deductions. If the dumbbell is not in the designated area and the dog breaks position to
retrieve while the “field assistant” is repositioning the dumbbell all points are taken, “M” 0 pts.
Basic position in front of the hurdle and scaling wall
The distance of the basic position of the handler in front of the hurdle and scaling wall must be marked at about 4 meters. This is the minimum distance for the basic position for these exercises.
The handler is allowed to take his/her basic position behind this line.

🏆 Score: ☕ GOOD — stay at the current grade

This sounds like a solid learning session, but not an advance yet, because Java clearly understands the basic finish concept while the exact geometry is still variable.

🐕 Dog observations

The big thing is she gets the fucking game now. 🎯 She’s returning to finish and can do it without food in your hand, which is a nice confirmation that the behavior isn’t dependent on seeing the lure.

But now that the broad behavior is understood, you’re seeing the smaller errors clearly:

* sometimes over-tucked
* sometimes too far forward
* otherwise finding the finish correctly

That’s exactly the point where I would tighten what earns the good paycheck rather than adding difficulty.

🎯 Focus and goals

Your instinct about the balance is right:

Fun atmosphere ≠ loose technical criterion.

You don’t need to choose between “WOOHOO FOOD CHASE!” and “your ass belongs HERE.” 😂

That’s actually the skill you’re trying to develop as a handler right now: hold a precise criterion without becoming Precision Robot Mother.

Happy Hound/Bil-Jac flying around while you’re reloading is great because it keeps the session active. Then when Java comes into finish, you can still look at the actual answer and decide whether that particular geometry is what you want.

⚡ One Fix

Now that she understands the exercise, make the best finishes more profitable than the merely recognizable finishes.

Correct location + straight rear = 💥 YES, raw food / bigger event.

Slightly over-tucked or too far forward = don’t pretend it’s perfect just because you’re pleased she’s understanding the concept. Reset/reorganize as needed and give her another opportunity.

That is exactly how you avoid the two shitty extremes:

🔥 Fun but sloppy versus 🎯 precise but emotionally dead.

You’re building 🔥 + 🎯.

📈 Trends

This is actually progressing nicely from the earlier finish work. Java has moved from figuring out where the hell she belongs toward refining exactly where she belongs.

And importantly, you’re changing your old precision-training pattern at the same time: throwing food, moving, keeping things upbeat, then asking for technical accuracy.

That’s exactly the experiment we wanted.

✅ Successes

Big wins: she understands the finish concept, food visibly in your hand is already becoming unnecessary, you’re maintaining movement/fun between repetitions, and you’re noticing subtle geometry instead of just rewarding “approximately beside me.”

That’s a productive fucking session. ☕

⚠️ Problems

The over-tuck matters just as much as being out. We don’t want to solve ass-out by creating ass-in. 😂

And being too far forward is its own spatial criterion. So don’t lump every error into “tuck.” At this point Java needs to learn the whole location, not simply more rear-end movement = better.

🔥 Key insight

You’re entering the refinement phase of this component.

Earlier, helping and accepting approximations made sense because Java was learning the motor solution.

Now she’s telling you:

“Yeah, yeah, I know I’m supposed to put my ass somewhere over here.”

😂

Cool. Now the answer becomes:

“Correct. And THIS exact version is the one that pays best.”

🧠 Handler observations

I really like that you’re consciously thinking about both emotional atmosphere and technical criterion simultaneously.

That’s the handler skill you’re trying to rebuild.

You don’t have to become serious to notice she’s 2 inches too far forward.

Notice it. Fix the criterion. Then go back to throwing fucking Bil-Jac around the garage. 😂🔥

🚀 Next session plan

Same grade. Don’t add duration, harder entries, more formal heel, or anything else.

Keep the dynamic food throws/reloads. Ask for the same finish. Let her solve without food in the guiding hand when she can. Start preferentially paying the finishes where front-to-back position AND rear alignment are exactly what you want.

Once those good finishes become the default answer rather than one of several answers, then advance.

🐕 Java Says

“Yesterday Mother wanted my ass IN.”

“Today apparently there is such a thing as TOO IN.”

“I would like written specifications.” 🐕📐😂

🚫 Non-Negotiable For Next Session

Don’t lower the technical criterion in order to preserve fun.

Keep the fucking fun and insist that the best paycheck belongs to the exact finish you want.

The dog can move through the heeling game while simultaneously maintaining:

🔥 EMOTION / DRE
Active, animated, eager, forward, expressive, physically pushy/insistent, mobile/waggy and cognitively available. Excited rather than stalking. No barking. 

👀 ATTENTION
True eye contact/attention rather than reward/body targeting.

📍 POSITION / SPACE
Understands the dog’s space and handler’s space and responds appropriately to the handler’s movement.

🏃 MOVEMENT
Free, powerful, confident movement at the desired pace without leaning or mechanical stalking.

🎮 GAME
Entering heel does not predict the end of play. The dog can flow between heel, speed changes, running/chase, challenges and play without a major emotional category change.

🎰 REINFORCEMENT RESPONSE
Variable reward timing/magnitude makes the dog increasingly eager for another round rather than creating disengagement.
